component.name: Bible
component.summary: Read, compare and study the Bible offline

description.p: An offline Bible study app for GNOME. Download Bibles, commentaries and books from SWORD repositories once, then read without a connection.

ul.li: Read versions side by side
Highlight verses in named colours
Keep notes as plain Markdown files that work with Obsidian
See the commentary for the verse you are reading
Follow the church year on the Today page
Study the Greek and Hebrew word by word, with a lexicon
Read books, dictionaries and daily devotionals
Explore every cross-reference as a zoomable rainbow, ordered by date, writer, language, genre and more
See places on maps and events on a timeline, with Wikipedia introductions to every book
Listen to chapters, follow reading plans, and keep fasts and feasts

screenshot.caption: Today: the church year, your reading plan and the passage of the day
Reading with the Greek word by word, and a word's meaning underneath

ul.li: Fixed: choosing another Bible in the cross-reference views' version menu froze the app. A new automatic test switches Bibles there on every build.

Much more of the app in Spanish. Downloads, the Reading room, the reader and its panels, cross-references, the church fathers, the timeline, search, bookmarks and plans now follow the app's language; 260 strings are translated, up from 116. A few spots are still in English.

Church history articles offline. On Today, Save articles for offline downloads a short Wikipedia article for each church history event (the one Wikipedia's search finds closest), and Read shows it without the internet.

Reinstall from Downloads. Modules you downloaded show a Reinstall button in Browse, which downloads them again over the old copy: handy for a module that's damaged, or a map module installed before its pictures came along.
The Reading room has a section list on the left with counts (Books, Devotionals, Dictionaries, Church fathers, the Quran), like Downloads.
Books in the Reading room get a Contents panel beside the text, with a search box and the current section highlighted, like the church fathers and the Quran.
Change the Bible in the cross-reference views with the new version menu in the header, without going back to the reader. It changes your reading Bible too, so both stay in step.
Cross-references are worked out again when a Bible is updated, and old saved copies are cleared away instead of piling up.
A book page whose pictures weren't downloaded (modules installed before 0.9.21) now says so, with a button to Downloads.

Behind the scenes: the Quran download is now tested against Tanzil on every build, a download site that's briefly down no longer holds up a release, and the code is split into smaller, steadier pieces.

Bible references in Wikipedia articles open in the app. Tap a reference such as John 3:16 in a book's introduction to go straight to it; the articles' other links no longer open the browser. This works for articles you've already saved too.
The map covers the whole world, so far-off places such as Tarshish, Cush, Sheba and India sit on real land (Natural Earth, public domain).
Zoom buttons on the map, and smoother zooming with a touchpad: you can always zoom back in, or show all places again.

Maps and pictures now download with their modules. Downloads from CrossWire's main library now fetch the module's complete package, so the picture files that map and atlas modules need come along. If you already installed one (such as the SonLight maps), remove it and download it again to get its pictures.

Maps and pictures in books. Books and dictionaries that include pictures (maps, illustrations) now show them under the text in the Reading room, fitted to the page. The pictures come from the module itself.

How literally each Bible translates. In Downloads, Bibles now show whether they translate word for word, balanced, thought for thought, or as a paraphrase, as classified in Wikipedia's article on dynamic and formal equivalence. Bibles that article doesn't list show no such tag.
The website now thanks and links CrossWire, the SWORD Project and eBible.org, where most downloads come from.

Many more cross-references from older-format Bibles. Bibles such as the ISV list their cross-references in the text rather than in notes; these are now read as cross-references, including lists like "1 Chr 22:10; 28:6" where the book isn't repeated. The ISV goes from about 400 to over 16,000 in the rainbow, and shows them as † notes while reading.

Every CrossWire category in Downloads. Maps and pictures have their own category, and texts CrossWire files under other traditions (such as the Book of Mormon) are listed last under Other traditions instead of among the Bibles.

The rainbow uses your Bible's own cross-references whenever it has any, even an incomplete set (ESV, for example, brings over 85,000). The built-in OpenBible.info set is used only for Bibles with none of their own, and the footer says which you're seeing.

Tags on Bibles in Downloads. Up to three short tags say what a Bible can do: Cross-references (used by the rainbow), Word study (Strong's), Footnotes, Red letters or Headings. They come straight from each module's own description on the download server.
Bibles with their own cross-references are marked in Downloads with an "Own cross-references" tag; the rainbow and the other views use those links.

Flatpak: your downloads stay when you update. Every release now checks this, along with the window opening with the splash screen on. (The re-downloads in the last few versions came from moving Flatpak downloads into the app's own folder in 0.9.11, and the Quran's new pronunciation in 0.9.13; neither repeats.)
In the Reading room, the Quran has its own section at the bottom instead of appearing under the church fathers.
The Quran's pronunciation shows long and emphatic letters underlined, as Tanzil marks them, instead of showing raw tags.

Contents as a panel. In the Reading room, a book's contents (each surah of the Quran, each section of the church fathers) now sit in a panel beside the text, with the part you're reading highlighted. The Contents button shows or hides it.

How the Arabic sounds. Each verse of the Quran now shows its pronunciation in Latin letters under the Arabic (Tanzil's transliteration), as the Greek and Hebrew do. Download the Quran again to get it.
Islamic history in the timeline, as its own lane: from the Prophet's life and the Hijra through the caliphates, Córdoba, the House of Wisdom, the Ottomans and the Mughals.

Cross-references from your Bible. When the selected Bible comes with its own full set of cross-references, the rainbow and the other views now use them. Otherwise the footer says plainly that the links are OpenBible.info's set, which is built into the app (so it works offline too).

The Quran, for study and comparison. Downloads, Start here, has the Quran at the very bottom: the Arabic text (Tanzil) with Marmaduke Pickthall's English translation (1930), verse by verse, read in the Reading room. Story links with the Bible and the cross-reference views come later.

Ready for Flathub. In the Flatpak, downloads now go into the app's own folder, so it needs no access to your home folder; the update banner is gone there, since GNOME Software updates Flatpaks; and the app's store listing has screenshots and every version's notes.
The language list in Downloads no longer jumps around as you scroll.

Word details live inside Original. Tap a Greek or Hebrew word and its meaning, grammar and lexicon entry open right under the interlinear, instead of in a separate Words tab. The lexicon comes with the Greek and Hebrew download, so nothing else is needed.
Church history on Today has a button on each event to read about it on Wikipedia.
Every release now checks that the files Bible offers to download (Bible sources, Greek and Hebrew data, church fathers, audio, Wikipedia) are still reachable.

Personal copies. Many modern translations are still under copyright, so they can't be offered for download. If you already have one as a SWORD module (.zip), add it from Downloads, Start here, Personal copies. It stays on your computer.
Plans for reading the Quran and seeing its story parallels with the Bible (in docs/quran.md); not in the app yet.

Downloads, a category at a time. Browse now has a list on the left: Start here, Bibles, Commentaries, Books, Devotionals, and Dictionaries and lexicons, each with a count. Search still looks through everything.
Languages by name. The language menu shows every language's name instead of codes such as "ckb" or "tpi", in alphabetical order, with how many works each has, and you can type to find one.
A little more space under the search bar.

Mac app (untested): the macOS download is now a real Bible.app with everything inside it, GTK included, so nothing else needs installing (Apple Silicon). Unzip, drag it to Applications, and allow it once in System Settings, Privacy & Security, since it isn't notarized by Apple.

Windows build (untested): text uses Windows' own fonts (Georgia or Cambria for scripture, Cascadia Mono or Consolas for code) instead of falling back to a plain sans font, and the app's own icons are included. No more console window beside the app, and no "win32 session" warning. The zip's README explains the SmartScreen warning: the app isn't code-signed.

Bible is made for GNOME first: Windows and macOS builds are offered as they are, without support. Bug reports now use a short form, and reports from Windows or macOS are closed automatically with a note.
The original-language button reads Αω (Alpha and Omega).
The README says plainly that Windows and macOS builds are untested; Bible is made for GNOME first. (This release has no Windows build: its font check failed, and it was fixed in 0.9.7.)
